info.name: Chronoloop B1 — Auth Flow (Local)
info.description:
End-to-end walkthrough of the B1 auth flow against the local chronoloop-backend dev server (http://localhost:4000).

**Run order matters.** Requests are numbered 01–11 and must be sent top to bottom (or via Collection Runner) because each one depends on state (tokens, IDs) captured by the ones before it.

**Two manual steps required** (the mailer is stubbed — it logs instead of sending real email):
- Before **04. Accept Invite**, copy the invite token from the `pnpm dev` console into the `inviteToken` collection variable.
- Before **07. Reset Password**, copy the reset token from the `pnpm dev` console into the `resetToken` collection variable.

Exact instructions are in each of those requests' description tabs.

**Why tokens are captured in variables instead of relying on Postman's cookie jar:** the backend's refresh-token cookie is set with `Secure; SameSite=None` (correct behavior — matches production, where frontend and backend are different HTTPS origins). Postman's cookie jar does not send `Secure` cookies over plain `http://localhost`, so relying on it would silently break every request after login. Instead, each request that receives a `Set-Cookie: refreshToken=...` header captures the raw value into the `refreshToken` collection variable via its Tests script, and requests that need to send it back do so with an explicit `Cookie: refreshToken={{refreshToken}}` header — this works regardless of the Secure flag since it's just a normal header, not the cookie jar.

exec: // Generate fresh, unique identifiers each time this request is sent, so the
// whole collection can be re-run repeatedly without hitting 409 EMAIL_ALREADY_REGISTERED.
pm.test('Response has accessToken, user, and workspace', () => {

request.description:
Creates User 1 (as workspace OWNER) and a new Workspace in one transaction.

Captures `accessToken`, `workspaceId`, and the raw `refreshToken` (from Set-Cookie) into collection variables for later steps.

The pre-request script generates fresh, timestamp-suffixed `user1Email` / `user2Email` / `workspaceName` values every time this request is sent, so you can click Send on this request again (or re-run the whole collection) without a 409 EMAIL_ALREADY_REGISTERED.
Confirms the access token from step 01 works and returns User 1's own profile.

exec: pm.test('Invite created for the right email/role', () => {

request.description:
Invites User 2 into the workspace as a MEMBER, sent by User 1 (OWNER).

**Manual step before the next request:** the invite token is never returned in this response (only its hash is stored server-side) — the mailer is stubbed and just logs it. Look in the terminal running `pnpm dev` for a block like:

```
[mailer stub] to=member+169...@example.com subject="You've been invited to join a Chronoloop workspace"
Accept your invite: http://localhost:5173/accept-invite?token=THIS_IS_THE_TOKEN
```

Copy the value after `token=` (a 64-character hex string) and paste it into this collection's `inviteToken` variable (Collection → Variables tab, or the environment quick-look eye icon → Current Value) before sending **04. Accept Invite**.

exec: throw new Error('inviteToken collection variable is empty — copy it from the pnpm dev console output for the previous request (see that request\'s description) before sending this one.');

request.description:
Accepts the invite using the token you pasted into `inviteToken` (see step 03's description). Creates User 2, adds them as a MEMBER of the workspace, and logs them in (returns an accessToken, sets a refreshToken cookie).

The pre-request script will fail loudly with a clear error if `inviteToken` is still blank.

exec: pm.test('Status is 403 (MEMBER cannot manage workspace settings)', () => {

request.description: User 2 (MEMBER role) attempts to rename the workspace. `requireRole('MANAGE_WORKSPACE_SETTINGS')` only permits OWNER/ADMIN, so this must return 403 FORBIDDEN — confirms role-based authorization is actually enforced, not just membership.

Requests a password reset for User 1. Always returns the same generic 200 message whether or not the email exists (enumeration-hardened) — that's expected, not a bug.

**Manual step before the next request:** look in the `pnpm dev` console for a block like:

```
[mailer stub] to=owner+169...@example.com subject="Reset your Chronoloop password"
Reset your password: http://localhost:5173/reset-password?token=THIS_IS_THE_TOKEN
```

Copy the value after `token=` and paste it into this collection's `resetToken` variable before sending **07. Reset Password**.

exec: throw new Error('resetToken collection variable is empty — copy it from the pnpm dev console output for the previous request (see that request\'s description) before sending this one.');

request.description: Resets User 1's password using the token pasted into `resetToken` (see step 06's description). On success the server also revokes all of User 1's existing sessions server-side — so the refreshToken captured back in step 01 is now dead, which the next two steps rely on being replaced by a fresh login.

Confirms the password change from step 07 actually took effect by logging in with the new password. Captures a fresh `accessToken` and `refreshToken` for the refresh/logout tests below.

(If you want to also confirm the OLD password now fails, duplicate this request and swap `{{user1NewPassword}}` for `{{user1Password}}` — expect 401 INVALID_CREDENTIALS. Not included as a numbered step since the brief didn't ask for it.)

exec: pm.test('A rotated (different) refreshToken cookie is set', () => {

request.description: Sends the refresh token captured in step 08 as an explicit `Cookie` header (not via Postman's automatic cookie jar — see the collection description for why). Expects a new access token pair: the old refresh token is revoked server-side and a new one issued (rotate-on-use), which this request's Tests script captures and confirms is different from the one sent.

exec: // Deliberately NOT clearing the refreshToken collection variable here —
// the next request needs to replay this now-revoked value to confirm it's rejected.

request.description: Logs out using the (rotated) refresh token from step 09. Server revokes the session and clears the cookie. Expect an empty 204 response.

Replays the SAME refresh token that logout just revoked in 10a (the collection variable was deliberately left untouched). This must be rejected with 401 INVALID_REFRESH_TOKEN — confirms logout actually invalidates the session server-side rather than only clearing the client-side cookie.
